Multiple regression extends the simple linear model to **$p$ predictors**:
$$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \cdots + \beta_p X_p + \epsilon,$$
fitted by least squares. Each coefficient $b_i$ is interpreted with the other
predictors **held constant**: a one-unit increase in $X_i$ changes the
predicted response by $b_i$. Individual predictors are tested with
$t = b_i/SE$ on **$n-p-1$ error degrees of freedom**, and the whole model is
tested with the ANOVA **F-statistic** $F = (SSModel/p)/(SSE/(n-p-1))$ on
$p$ and $n-p-1$ df, with $H_0\colon\beta_1=\cdots=\beta_p=0$ (model
ineffective) vs $H_a\colon$ at least one $\beta_i \neq 0$ (model effective).
**$R^2 = SSModel/SSTotal$** is the percent of response variability explained
by all predictors together, and **adjusted $R^2$** $=1-(1-R^2)\frac{n-1}{n-p-1}$
penalizes model size. Binary categorical predictors enter as **indicator
(dummy) variables** coded 0/1, giving parallel lines. All fits below use
numpy least squares via the helper `multi_reg` (coefficient table with
standard errors, t- and p-values, plus the full ANOVA table), and — per this
project's convention — every parametric F-test on real data is re-checked
with a **randomization test** (`perm_F`: shuffle the response, refit, recompute
$F$; 10000 shuffles, seed 2026). Exercises are from *Statistics: Unlocking
the Power of Data* (Lock⁵, 3rd ed., pp. 662–670): Skill Builders 10.1–10.22
dissect two printed multiple-regression outputs; the applied exercises
10.23–10.59 cover forest-fire damage, clinical depression scores, hours
hanging out with friends, home prices, calories, life expectancy, binary
predictors, race horses, hantavirus, golf scores, memory and texting, car
mileage, arm spans, mouse weight gain, NBA winning percentages, Mustang
prices, and a randomization test for the printer model.

```{python}
#| include: false
import os
from pathlib import Path
_root = Path.cwd()
while not (_root / "_quarto.yml").exists():
    _root = _root.parent
os.chdir(_root)
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

def multi_reg(X_df, y, names):
    """Least-squares multiple regression with numpy only.
    Returns dict: coefficient table, ANOVA table, summary, beta vector."""
    y = np.asarray(y, float)
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y)), np.asarray(X_df, float)])
    n, k = X.shape
    p = k - 1                       # number of predictors
    dfe = n - p - 1                 # error df
    beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
    resid = y - X @ beta
    sse = float(resid @ resid)
    sst = float(((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum())
    ssm = sst - sse
    s_e = float(np.sqrt(sse / dfe))
    se = np.sqrt(np.diag((sse / dfe) * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)))
    t = beta / se
    pval = 2 * stats.t.sf(np.abs(t), dfe)
    F = (ssm / p) / (sse / dfe)
    pF = float(stats.f.sf(F, p, dfe))
    R2 = ssm / sst
    adj = 1 - (1 - R2) * (n - 1) / dfe
    coef = pd.DataFrame({"Term": ["Intercept"] + list(names),
                         "Coef": np.round(beta, 4), "SE": np.round(se, 4),
                         "t": np.round(t, 3),
                         "p-value": [float(f"{v:.3g}") for v in pval]})
    anova = pd.DataFrame({"Source": ["Model", "Error", "Total"],
                          "df": [p, dfe, n - 1],
                          "SS": [round(ssm, 2), round(sse, 2), round(sst, 2)],
                          "MS": [round(ssm / p, 2), round(sse / dfe, 2), ""],
                          "F": [round(float(F), 3), "", ""],
                          "p-value": [float(f"{pF:.3g}"), "", ""]
                          }).set_index("Source")
    summ = pd.Series({"n": n, "predictors": p, "s_e": round(s_e, 4),
                      "R2": round(R2, 4), "adjR2": round(adj, 4),
                      "F": round(float(F), 3), "p-value": float(f"{pF:.3g}")})
    return {"coef": coef, "anova": anova, "summ": summ, "beta": beta,
            "s_e": s_e, "R2": R2, "n": n}

def perm_F(X_df, y, reps=10000, seed=2026):
    """Randomization F-test: shuffle the response, refit the model,
    recompute F each time. (Refitting by least squares is equivalent to
    applying the hat matrix H = X(X'X)^-1 X' to the shuffled response.)"""
    y = np.asarray(y, float)
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y)), np.asarray(X_df, float)])
    n, k = X.shape
    p = k - 1
    dfe = n - p - 1
    H = X @ np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T
    def F_of(yy):
        sse = float(((yy - H @ yy) ** 2).sum())
        sst = float(((yy - yy.mean()) ** 2).sum())
        return ((sst - sse) / p) / (sse / dfe)
    Fobs = F_of(y)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    sims = np.empty(reps)
    for i in range(reps):
        sims[i] = F_of(rng.permutation(y))
    return sims, float(Fobs), float((sims >= Fobs).mean())

def sim_hist(sims, obs, xlabel="Simulated F-statistics", bins=40,
             figsize=(6, 3)):
    """Histogram of simulated statistics with the observed one marked."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    sns.histplot(x=sims, bins=bins, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
    mask = sims >= obs
    if mask.any():
        sns.histplot(x=sims[mask], bins=bins, ax=ax, color="#c44e52")
    ax.axvline(obs, color="black", lw=1.5)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel); ax.set_ylabel("Simulated statistics")
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Exercise 10.23

*(Predicting Area Burned by a Forest Fire)* The model uses **ForestFires**
($n = 517$ Portuguese fires) to predict burned area (hectares) from Wind,
Temp, RH and Rain. Fitting live reproduces the book's output exactly
($s_\epsilon = 63.53$, $R^2 = 1.17\%$, $F = 1.51$, p = 0.197):

```{python}
ff = pd.read_csv("data/ch10/ForestFires.csv")
ff_fit = multi_reg(ff[["Wind", "Temp", "RH", "Rain"]], ff["Area"],
                   ["Wind", "Temp", "RH", "Rain"])
print(ff_fit["coef"].to_string(index=False)); print()
print(ff_fit["anova"].to_string()); print()
print(ff_fit["summ"].to_string())
```

**(a)** From the printed equation, a fire with Wind = 8.5 km/h, Temp =
4.6°C, RH = 21%, Rain = 0:

```{python}
#| echo: false
yhat = -6.4 + 1.28*8.5 + 1.010*4.6 - 0.110*21 - 2.83*0
print(f"predicted area = {yhat:.2f} hectares")
```

**Predicted area burned $\approx$ 6.82 hectares.**
**(b)** Residual $= 10.73 - 6.82 =$ **3.91 hectares** (this fire burned
about 3.9 ha more than predicted).

## Exercise 10.26

*(Is the Model Effective at Predicting Area Burned?)*

**(a)** **F = 1.51** with df $(4, 512)$, **p-value = 0.197**.
**(b)** Generic conclusion: the data do not give enough evidence to reject
$H_0\colon\beta_1=\cdots=\beta_4=0$; in context, atmospheric conditions
(wind, temperature, humidity, rain) show **no significant overall
relationship** with area burned. Randomization check (10000 shuffles of the
response, seed 2026) agrees:

```{python}
sims, Fobs, p_perm = perm_F(ff[["Wind", "Temp", "RH", "Rain"]], ff["Area"])
print(f"observed F = {Fobs:.3f},  randomization p-value = {p_perm:.4f}")
```

**(c)** **No** — the model is not effective (p = 0.197, and $R^2$ is only
1.17%).

## Exercise 10.27

*(Analyzing the Model Predicting Area Burned)* **$R^2 = 1.17\%$**: the four
atmospheric variables together explain only **1.17%** of the variation in
area burned by forest fires (adjusted $R^2 = 0.40\%$).

**Predicted CESD $\approx$ 24.55.**

points *below* predicted).

## Exercise 10.33

*(Predicting Hours Hanging Out with Friends)* The model uses **PASeniors**
($n = 439$ students with complete data) to predict HangHours from six
activity variables. Fitting live reproduces the book's output exactly
($s_\epsilon = 9.96$, $R^2 = 13.43\%$, F = 11.17):

```{python}
ps = pd.read_csv("data/ch09/PASeniors.csv")
hang_cols = ["HangHours", "HWHours", "SportsHours", "VideoGameHours",
             "ComputerHours", "TVHours", "WorkHours"]
hangsub = ps.dropna(subset=hang_cols)
hang_fit = multi_reg(hangsub[hang_cols[1:]], hangsub["HangHours"],
                     hang_cols[1:])
print(hang_fit["coef"].to_string(index=False)); print()
print(hang_fit["summ"].to_string())
```

Using the printed equation for the two cases in Table 10.1:

```{python}
#| echo: false
for tag, hw, sp, vg, cp, tv, wk, obs in [("Case 1", 0.25, 6.0, 0.0, 2.0, 2.0, 8.0, 12.0),
                                         ("Case 2", 21.0, 2.0, 0.0, 15.0, 3.0, 0.0, 2.0)]:
    yhat = (5.84 - 0.1003*hw + 0.3305*sp + 0.0775*vg
            + 0.0804*cp + 0.2177*tv + 0.0832*wk)
    print(f"{tag}: predicted = {yhat:.2f},  residual = {obs - yhat:+.2f}")
```

**(a) Case 1:** predicted **9.06 hours**, residual $= 12 - 9.06 =$ **+2.94**.
**(b) Case 2:** predicted **6.25 hours**, residual $= 2 - 6.25 =$ **$-4.25$**.

## Exercise 10.38

*(Predicting Prices of Homes)* Output for **HomesForSale** ($n = 120$ homes
from several states): $\text{Price} = 103.75 + 0.082\,\text{Size}
- 25.81\,\text{Beds} + 84.96\,\text{Baths}$, with
$s_\epsilon = 228.1$, $R^2 = 19.5\%$, adjusted $R^2 = 17.5\%$; ANOVA:
Model df $= 3$, SS $= 1464285$, F $= 9.38$, P $= 0.00001$; Error df $= 116$.
Price is in \$1000s, Size in square feet.

**(a)** For 2500 sq ft, 4 bedrooms, 2.5 baths:

```{python}
#| echo: false
yhat = 103.75 + 0.082*2500 - 25.81*4 + 84.96*2.5
print(f"predicted price = {yhat:.2f} thousand dollars")
```

**Predicted price $\approx$ \$417.9 thousand (about \$418,000).**

**(b)** Largest coefficient in magnitude: **Baths** (84.96).
**(c)** Most important: **Baths** — it is the only predictor with a
significant t-statistic ($t = 2.46$, p = 0.015). (Coefficient magnitudes
cannot be compared directly: Size is per square foot while Beds/Baths are
per room.)
**(d)** Significant at 5%: **Baths only** (p = 0.015); Size just misses
(p = 0.057) and Beds is not significant (p = 0.433).
**(e)** Each additional square foot of size adds **0.082 thousand dollars
(\$82)** to the predicted price, holding number of bedrooms and bathrooms
constant.
**(f)** The ANOVA F = 9.38 with p $\approx$ 0.00001: reject $H_0$ — the
model **is effective**; size, bedrooms and bathrooms together help predict
price.
**(g)** **$R^2 = 19.5\%$**: the three predictors together explain 19.5% of
the variation in home prices.

**(a)** For a 35-year-old eating 40 g fat and 180 mg cholesterol:

```{python}
#| echo: false
yhat = 512.95 + 16.2645*40 + 0.4208*180 - 1.420*35
print(f"predicted calories = {yhat:.1f}")
```

**Predicted daily intake $\approx$ 1190 calories.**

**(b)** Least significant: **Age** (p = 0.277); most significant: **Fat**
(p = 0.000, $t = 20.5$).
**(c)** Significant at 5%: **Fat** and **Cholesterol** (p = 0.038).
**(d)** Each additional gram of fat consumed per day is associated with
about **16 more calories** consumed, holding cholesterol and age constant.
**(e)** Each additional year of age is associated with about **1.4 fewer
calories** consumed per day, holding fat and cholesterol constant (not
significant).
**(f)** F = 336.12 with p $\approx$ 0.000: the model **is effective** —
reject $H_0$; at least one of fat, cholesterol and age helps predict
calorie consumption.
**(g)** **$R^2 = 76.4\%$**: fat, cholesterol and age together explain
76.4% of the variation in daily calories consumed.

## Exercise 10.52

*(Predicting HwyMPG)* Using **Cars2020** ($n = 110$ cars), comparing three
models for HwyMPG:

```{python}
cars = pd.read_csv("data/ch09/Cars2020.csv")
cars_city = multi_reg(cars[["CityMPG"]], cars["HwyMPG"], ["CityMPG"])
cars_weight = multi_reg(cars[["Weight"]], cars["HwyMPG"], ["Weight"])
cars_both = multi_reg(cars[["CityMPG", "Weight"]], cars["HwyMPG"],
                      ["CityMPG", "Weight"])
print("R2, CityMPG alone:        ",
      f"{cars_city['R2']:.3f}  (s_e = {cars_city['s_e']:.2f})")
print("R2, Weight alone:         ",
      f"{cars_weight['R2']:.3f}  (s_e = {cars_weight['s_e']:.2f})")
print("R2, CityMPG + Weight:     ",
      f"{cars_both['R2']:.3f}  (s_e = {cars_both['s_e']:.2f})")
print()
print(cars_both["coef"].to_string(index=False))
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
sims, Fobs, p_perm = perm_F(cars[["CityMPG", "Weight"]], cars["HwyMPG"])
print(f"two-predictor model: observed F = {Fobs:.3f}, "
      f"randomization p-value = {p_perm:.4f}")
```

**(a)** CityMPG alone explains **76.9%** of the variability in HwyMPG.
**(b)** Weight alone explains **66.8%**.
**(c)** Together they explain **78.3%** ($F = 192.9$; randomization p
$< 0.001$).
**(d)** Both coefficients remain significant in the two-predictor model
(CityMPG $t = 7.53$, p < 0.001; Weight $t = -2.61$, p = 0.011), and adding
Weight to CityMPG raises $R^2$ from 76.9% to 78.3% while cutting
$s_\epsilon$ from 3.47 to 3.38 mpg — a real but **modest** gain, so
CityMPG does most of the work and Weight adds only a little unique
information (the two are strongly related: heavier cars get worse city
mileage).

## Exercise 10.58

*(Comparing Models for NBA Winning Percentage)*

**(a)** Comparing the $R^2$s from the three fits above: **PtsFor alone
43.7%, PtsAgainst alone 29.2%, both together 96.1%** — the multiple
regression explains far more than either single predictor.

**(b)** New predictor Diff $=$ PtsFor $-$ PtsAgainst:

```{python}
nba["Diff"] = nba["PtsFor"] - nba["PtsAgainst"]
nba_diff = multi_reg(nba[["Diff"]], nba["WinPct"], ["Diff"])
print(nba_diff["coef"].to_string(index=False)); print()
print(nba_diff["summ"].to_string())
```

```{python}
sims, Fobs, p_perm = perm_F(nba[["Diff"]], nba["WinPct"])
print(f"observed F = {Fobs:.3f},  randomization p-value = {p_perm:.4f}")
b = nba_diff["beta"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 3.4))
ax.scatter(nba["Diff"], nba["WinPct"], color="#4c72b0", alpha=0.75)
xs = np.linspace(nba["Diff"].min(), nba["Diff"].max(), 50)
ax.plot(xs, b[0] + b[1]*xs, color="#c44e52", lw=2)

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

two-predictor model (96.1%, $s_\epsilon = 0.030$). The point differential
captures virtually all the information in the two separate scoring rates;
the relationship is very linear with Toronto (Diff $= 6.0$) and the other
playoff teams at the upper right.

                   ["PhotoTime", "CostColor"])
print(ip_fit["coef"].to_string(index=False)); print()
print(ip_fit["summ"].to_string())
```

Randomizing the 20 prices over the PhotoTime/CostColor combinations
(10000 shuffles, seed 2026):

```{python}
sims, Fobs, p_perm = perm_F(ip[["PhotoTime", "CostColor"]], ip["Price"])
p_F = stats.f.sf(Fobs, 2, 17)
print(f"observed F = {Fobs:.3f}")
print(f"F-distribution p-value (df = 2, 17): {p_F:.4f}")
print(f"randomization p-value: {p_perm:.4f}")
sim_hist(sims, Fobs)
```

The observed $F = 6.30$ sits firmly in the upper tail of the randomization
distribution: the **randomization p-value $\approx$ 0.009** agrees closely
with the **$F_{2,17}$ p-value $\approx$ 0.009**. The F-distribution
approximates the randomization distribution very well here, and both
indicate the printer model is effective (p < 0.05).

:::
